taxonomy.note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; Texas is within the native range. Historical var. pumila is included in the species concept.

evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Dalea enneandra as native in Texas.
USDA PLANTS-derived county native-status data records Dalea enneandra as native in Bell County.
The same USDA county dataset records it as native in Burnet County.
The same USDA county dataset records it as native in Comal County; additional target-zone native counties include Gillespie, Kerr, San Saba, Travis, and Williamson.
target_zone_range.guardrail: County entries are used only where the source explicitly carries native status; generic occurrence-only records are not substituted.

morphology.look_here_first: Look at spacing along the flower spike: D. enneandra has a long slender, often nodding or drooping spike where the flowers and broad bracts are visibly separated instead of packed into a dense cone.
diagnostic_traits: erect herbaceous perennial, usually with one to a few stems branching above
odd-pinnate leaves with narrow linear to narrowly oblong leaflets
terminal slender spike, commonly elongate and looser than the dense-headed Dalea in this batch
flowers sessile or nearly sessile and visibly spaced along the rachis
broad conspicuous bracts remain an important spike-level cue
nine stamens provide a technical reproductive confirmation

confusers.separator: D. compacta packs flowers into a dense swollen cylindrical/ovoid head; D. enneandra shows open spacing along a slender spike.
D. aurea has a densely villous fuzzy head and silky leaves; D. enneandra has a much looser spike and narrower less-silky leaflets.
D. purpurea forms a compact dense prairie-clover spike; D. enneandra's widely separated flowers/bracts make the rachis much more obvious.
